title: Signs of the Spirit (CCC 694–701)
hookLine: water, anointing, fire, cloud, seal, hand, finger and dove

cards: On the table: a pitcher of water. A small bottle of oil. A lit candle.
A stamp and some sealing wax. A drawing of a bird. It could be a craft-store receipt.

It's actually the Catechism's list for talking about someone nobody can see. The Holy Spirit has no face in the Gospels and no human body. Jesus compares the Spirit to the wind, which you hear but can't trace.
So scripture keeps reaching for things you can hold, burn, pour and watch fly.

teach.b: Day three hundred seven met the Spirit as the Paraclete; today, the Spirit's pictures. The Catechism walks through them one by one, and several show up again in Catholic worship.
Water first: Jesus speaks of being born again of water and the Holy Ghost, so baptism pours it. Then anointing with oil.
Christ means anointed, and the Catechism says the Spirit is the anointing; Catholics are anointed with chrism at baptism and confirmation. Then fire, which transforms whatever it touches.
At Pentecost, in the Douay-Rheims, "there appeared to them parted tongues as it were of fire, and it sat upon every one of them."
Then cloud and light: the cloud on Mount Sinai, the cloud at the Transfiguration, and the word overshadow from Mary's story.
Then the seal, close to anointing, a mark that stays; the Catechism links it to the sacraments that can't be repeated. Then the hand.
Jesus heals by laying on hands, and the apostles give the Spirit the same way; the Church keeps that gesture in its sacraments. Then the finger.
Jesus says he casts out devils by the finger of God, and the Catechism remembers that the law was written on stone by God's finger, and is now written by the Spirit on human hearts. Last, the dove.
After the flood, Noah's dove comes back with a fresh olive branch.
At the Jordan, as Jesus comes up from the water, Matthew says he saw the Spirit of God descending as a dove.

teach.h: PARTED TONGUES AS IT WERE OF FIRE.
teach.b: So the list runs between two pictures of one Spirit: fire that changes things, and a dove that settles and brings peace.

how: In Catholic worship the Spirit's signs are used, not only described: water at baptism, chrism at baptism and confirmation, the laying on of hands at confirmation and ordination, and the Easter candle's fire.

games.q: what does “signs of the spirit” mean?
o: miracles that prove a person is truly a saint
lucky charms that bring down the Spirit's favor
pictures of the Spirit: water, oil, fire, a dove

games.q: signs of the Spirit — tap the pairs.
p: born again of water and the Holy Ghost
the law written on stone, then hearts
at the Jordan, and with Noah's olive branch

s: the Gospels describe the Holy Spirit as having a human body
the Spirit appears in signs: fire, cloud, a dove.
the Catechism connects anointing with the title Christ
Christ means anointed, and the Spirit is the anointing.
the Spirit's signs are only images in old stories
water, chrism and the laying on of hands are still used in the sacraments.

games.q: some in the crowd say Jesus casts out devils by the prince of devils. what does he say he casts them out by?
games.why: Luke has him say it is "by the finger of God", and if so, the kingdom of God has come upon them. the Catechism counts the finger among the Spirit's signs.

practice: Let the list pass by slowly, water, oil, fire, cloud and light, a seal, a hand, a finger, a dove, and stay with whichever one catches: water, maybe, because you showered this morning, or a hand, because someone held yours this week.
Ask what it shows about something you can't see. If you pray, ask the Spirit to come in that form today; if you don't, keep that image close.

wordCard.voice: Signs of the Spirit. Scripture's pictures for the God no one can see, still used in the sacraments. Today's word.

orig.note: the Greek word for dove in the Gospel accounts of Jesus's baptism.

carryVoice: Your line: fire and dove. Pictures you can hold, for someone you can't. Rest well.
